title: Carrying a gun: ground, car and home
summary: How to carry a gun at a Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting ground, take it by car and keep it at home, and where to read about trips abroad. Laws differ between countries.

body.html: Let us start at the ground. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting a gun is carried open (a semi-automatic with the breech open), with the muzzle pointing straight up or straight down. Slings are not allowed. When the gun is not in your hands, it stands upright in a gun rack, and nobody touches another shooter's gun without permission.

Away from the ground, the law of the country applies. Almost everywhere you need a licence or permit for a shotgun, and the rules for transport and storage differ even between neighbouring countries. Before a trip, check the rules of the destination and of any transit country, several weeks in advance.
By car, the gun travels unloaded, in a case or slip, out of sight, and in many countries separately from the cartridges. Do not leave a gun in a car unattended.

At home, keep the gun as your country's law requires, usually locked in a safe and out of reach of children. Many laws also ask for cartridges to be stored separately. Care and storage: Care and cleaning.

Going abroad with your own gun? The European Firearms Pass is issued only to residents of EU countries and of Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, which apply the same EU firearms rules. It is used for travel with your own gun. Others usually need a permit from the destination country or hire a gun there.
Details are in the Travel block: Travelling with a gun inside the EU, Outside the EU: national permits and Flying with a gun.

Keep your documents together and at hand: the licence or permit, the pass or temporary permit, the competition invitation and any travel confirmations. At a border or an airport, answer calmly and precisely.

key_points.html: At the ground the gun is open, muzzle up or down, with no sling.
Firearms laws differ between countries; check them weeks in advance.
By car: unloaded, in a case, out of sight, often apart from the cartridges.
The European Firearms Pass is only for residents of EU and Schengen countries travelling with their own gun.
Keep all documents together and at hand.

did_you_know.html: Because a gun that is not in use must stand upright in a rack, many grounds put a gun rack next to each stand. That way nobody lays a gun on the ground or leans it against a fence.

quiz.q: How is a gun carried at the ground?

options.text: Closed, on a sling over the shoulder
Open, with the muzzles up or down
Closed, but with the safety catch on
Any way at all, if it is unloaded

quiz.explain: The rules require the gun to be carried open, muzzle straight up or down; slings are not allowed.

quiz.q: How does a gun usually travel by car?

options.text: Loaded, on the back seat, ready to use
Assembled, in a roof box with the bags
In the cartridge bag, with the boxes
Unloaded, in a case and out of sight

quiz.explain: Unloaded, cased and out of sight; many countries also require the cartridges to travel separately.

quiz.q: Who can get a European Firearms Pass?

options.text: A resident of an EU or Schengen country who owns the gun
Any shooter with a competition invitation
Anyone who books a trip with a coach
Only members of a national team

quiz.explain: The pass is issued by the EU or Schengen country where you live, for your own guns. Shooters from other countries need other permits or hire a gun.
